reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / IDSA
clinicalPearls: Driven by invasive group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) whose exotoxins act as superantigens, provoking massive cytokine release and rapid-onset shock
Frequently arises from a soft-tissue focus such as necrotising fasciitis or cellulitis, though a portal of entry is not always evident
Pain out of proportion to visible skin findings is an early warning sign and should prompt urgent surgical assessment
Hypotension progresses quickly to multi-organ dysfunction, with renal impairment often preceding the drop in blood pressure
A generalised erythematous rash may be subtle or absent compared with staphylococcal toxic shock; desquamation can occur late

Management combines aggressive fluid resuscitation, prompt source control, and antibiotic principles pairing a beta-lactam with a protein-synthesis inhibitor such as clindamycin to switch off toxin production
Intravenous immunoglobulin is considered as an adjunct to neutralise circulating superantigens in severe disease
Mortality is high, so early recognition, critical-care support, and surgical debridement of any necrotising focus are decisive
reference.pathophysiology: Invasive strains of Streptococcus pyogenes release pyrogenic exotoxins and other superantigens that bind directly to MHC class II molecules and T-cell receptors outside the normal antigen groove. This triggers polyclonal T-cell activation and an overwhelming release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (a cytokine storm), producing capillary leak, vasodilatation, hypotension, and multi-organ failure. Bacteraemia and deep tissue invasion, often within necrotising soft-tissue infection, amplify the toxin load and accelerate the shock state.
additionalDifferentials: Septic shock from other Gram-positive or Gram-negative organisms
Severe drug reaction with systemic features
infectionMimics: Severe acute pancreatitis with systemic inflammatory response
additionalInvestigations: Blood cultures and cultures from any surgical or wound specimen
Serial lactate, renal and liver function, coagulation profile and creatine kinase to track organ involvement
Imaging (CT or MRI) of a suspected deep soft-tissue focus, without delaying surgery when necrotising infection is likely
Surgical exploration for tissue diagnosis when necrotising fasciitis is suspected
redFlags: Pain disproportionate to examination findings suggesting underlying necrotising infection requiring urgent debridement
Rapidly progressing hypotension and organ failure indicating established septic shock
Skin crepitus, bullae, dusky discolouration or rapidly advancing erythema pointing to deep tissue necrosis
Falling urine output and rising creatinine signalling early multi-organ dysfunction
reference.prognosis: Even with intensive treatment, mortality remains substantial and is highest when there is an associated necrotising soft-tissue infection or delayed source control; survival depends on early recognition, rapid surgery, and organ support.
pitfalls: Attributing severe limb pain to a minor injury and missing early necrotising infection
Relying on antibiotics alone without urgent surgical source control
Omitting a protein-synthesis inhibitor such as clindamycin, forgoing its anti-toxin effect
Underestimating fluid requirements and delaying critical-care escalation
